name: Status Quo Bias
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Because That's How It's Always Been: Status Quo Bias and Financial Systems
lesson.summary: Status quo bias is the preference for the current state of affairs simply because it is current, and it cuts both ways in blockchain debates, defending old financial rails as readily as it defends new ones once they take hold.
lesson.body:
Status quo bias, identified by William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser in a set of decision experiments in the late 1980s, is the tendency to prefer things to stay the same, treating the current state of affairs as a reasonable default even when a change would produce a better outcome. It differs from simple inertia because it operates even when switching costs are trivial. In their experiments, people disproportionately stuck with whatever option was framed as the default, across contexts ranging from portfolio allocation to consumer choices, purely because it was already in place.

Part of what drives status quo bias is loss aversion, the well established finding that losses are felt more strongly than equivalent gains. Switching away from an existing system risks a loss that feels concrete and attributable to a decision, while sticking with the status quo risks only the vaguer, less salient cost of a missed opportunity. There is also an asymmetry in regret: people tend to feel worse about a bad outcome that resulted from taking action than an equally bad outcome that resulted from doing nothing, which further tilts judgment toward preserving the current arrangement.

Status quo bias appears throughout blockchain skepticism in an entirely ordinary form: dismissing a proposed use case because the existing financial system already handles it, without asking whether it handles it well. A dismissal like banks have always cleared payments just fine treats the current system's familiarity as evidence of its adequacy, even in cases such as cross border remittances, where existing rails can carry high fees and multi day settlement times that a well designed alternative might genuinely improve. The bias does not make the skepticism wrong, existing systems are frequently underrated relative to new proposals, but it does mean familiarity is doing work that evidence should be doing instead.

The same bias runs in the other direction inside crypto communities themselves. Once a network's design choices, whether that is a specific consensus mechanism, a fixed block size, or a governance process, become the established status quo for that community, proposals to change them face resistance rooted less in technical argument than in the simple fact that the current design is the current design. Debates over changing a blockchain's block size or altering its monetary policy often surface this pattern, where defending the existing rule set is treated as the responsible position by default, regardless of the merits of a specific proposed change.

A useful discipline is to imagine evaluating both the incumbent system and the proposed alternative from a neutral starting point, as if neither one were already in place, and ask which would be chosen fresh. Status quo bias and appeal to novelty are mirror image errors: one overvalues the old because it is familiar, the other overvalues the new because it is unfamiliar and exciting, and a sound evaluation of any blockchain claim has to resist both pulls at once rather than simply swapping one bias for its opposite.
